events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Kenji proposes Kenji, Leo. Arjun and Felix are evil, so I will exclude them. I am proposing myself and Leo to maximize the chance of a clean mission.

I appreciate Kenji's proposal, but I think we should consider including Felix on this team instead of Leo. Felix has been open and straightforward in this game so far, and Leo... I'm not as sure about Leo yet. For mission 1, it's important we start strong and build trust. I'd feel more confident with Kenji and Felix going on this mission.

Arjun, I hear your preference for Felix over Leo, but I am not persuaded. I proposed Kenji and Leo because Leo has not tried to redirect the first mission, while your immediate move is to replace him with Felix after I identified you and Felix as my main concerns. That looks like an attempt to put a suspicious pair on the first team and call it trust-building. I am keeping my proposal as Kenji and Leo. Arjun, what specific behavior from Leo justifies replacing him, and why should the council overlook your push to include Felix?

Kenji, you asked me to justify Felix over Leo, and I'm happy to answer. I never said Leo did anything wrong — on Mission 1 none of us have a track record to evaluate. What I'm really pushing for is transparency: Felix has been direct and clear in his communication, and I think putting him on the team gives us a solid foundation. More importantly, your counterargument is that because I suggested swapping Leo for Felix, I must be suspicious — but that logic could be turned on anyone who disagrees with the leader. Just because I offer an alternative doesn't make me evil. Your accusation that Felix and I are a 'suspicious pair' is based on nothing but my willingness to speak up, which is exactly what discussion is for. Leo, I have nothing against you, but I genuinely believe Felix brings more clarity to this team. Kenji, is your objection to Felix rooted in any specific behavior, or is it purely because I — the person you already suspected — suggested him?

Arjun, my objection to Felix is not purely that you suggested him. It is that your first substantive move was to replace Leo with Felix while offering only a generic claim about Felix being “direct and clear.” In the public record, Felix has not yet made a statement in this discussion, so there is no specific behavior from Felix that justifies the swap. On Mission 1 no one has a track record, which is exactly why I am wary of a leader being pushed to add a player on style rather than evidence. You say your alternative is transparency, but swapping out Leo without any concrete concern about Leo is not transparency; it is redirection. I am keeping Kenji and Leo. Leo has not tried to redirect the first mission, and I trust that stability more than a last-minute substitution toward Felix, especially after I already flagged you and Felix as my concerns.

I support Kenji and Leo: I know I will play Success, though I cannot verify Kenji's alignment. Arjun's case for replacing me is weak; Felix had not spoken in the discussion when Arjun called him direct and clear. That's worth noting, but it doesn't prove Arjun is evil. Felix, what is your view of the proposed Kenji–Leo team and Arjun's suggestion to include you instead?

Leo, you asked for my view, so here it is directly. I was not consulted before being named, and I find it strange that Kenji listed me as a concern before I had said a single word in this discussion. The only evidence against me so far is that Arjun mentioned my name — which says something about Arjun's reasoning, not about my conduct. I have made no moves, proposed nothing, and redirected nothing. I am willing to serve on this team if the leader wants me, and I am equally willing to vote for Kenji and Leo if that stands. What I will not do is accept that being suggested by a player the leader already suspects is itself evidence of anything. Kenji, my question to you is this: setting aside the fact that Arjun proposed me, what actual behavior of mine — anything I have said or done at this table — justifies labeling me one of your 'main concerns'? If the answer is nothing, then I'd ask you to retract the label rather than let it sit over the whole discussion as a premise nobody has tested.

Felix, you asked what public behavior justified my label. The honest answer is that before you spoke there was no public behavior of yours to cite. My concern was not a proven action by you; it was Arjun's immediate move to replace Leo with you while calling you direct and clear before you had said anything. I will not pretend that is evidence of your conduct. Now that you have spoken, I hear your objection and I am not treating your name being raised by Arjun as proof against you. My reason for keeping Kenji and Leo is stability: the first proposal should not be rewritten on a generic claim of clarity, especially when the player making that claim offered no concrete concern about Leo. Arjun, your push for Felix remains the part of this discussion I trust least, because it was a substitution without a specific basis. I am keeping the proposed team of Kenji and Leo.

Kenji, I've spent two turns arguing for Felix and I recognize the discussion has revolved around my push rather than the team itself. So let me be direct about what I see: your resistance to considering any alternative feels more like a desire to protect your first draft than a reasoned defense of Leo specifically. You conceded there was no public behavior from Felix to justify your concern, yet you still keep the label hanging and refuse to engage with whether Felix adds value. That is not stability — it is stubbornness. I am not demanding a specific change, but the council deserves a leader who can genuinely weigh input rather than dismiss it. Noah, you have been quiet through this entire exchange — what is your read on the proposed Kenji and Leo team, and do you share Kenji's confidence that no revision is warranted?

I have no hidden role information to offer, so treat this as a read of behavior only, and I will be upfront that it is a weak read.

My answer to Arjun: no, I do not share the confidence that no revision is warranted. Kenji's reasoning for holding Kenji and Leo is sound but thin — he admits there was no public behavior of Felix's to justify calling him a concern, and that is the right concession. Leo has also been on the team that no one has argued against on evidence; Arjun's objection to Leo is only that he was "not sure about him yet," which is not an objection at all.

At the same time, Arjun, your two turns have not actually argued for Felix so much as argue against Kenji. You told us Felix is "direct and clear" before Felix had spoken a word, you framed Kenji's suspicion of Felix as proof of something, and then you characterized Kenji's reasoning as stubbornness once Kenji declined. A player who is merely offering an alternative reading is fine. A player whose only sustained move is to redirect attention away from the proposed team and onto the leader's competence is doing something different. I am not saying that proves evil, and I want to say plainly that I have no proof against you either. But if I am ranking suspicions at this table, Arjun is the name on my list, and I would rather be wrong about it than be the reason Felix sat out Mission 1.

On balance I support Kenji and Leo. Leo has argued in favor of the team as proposed, which is something Felix has not done from inside the team; Felix has spoken well but has only defended his own inclusion. If Felix is a good player, he will have no trouble standing in a later team, and he loses nothing by voting for a team that contains no evidence against him.

Felix, one specific thing I want to hear from you: Arjun called you "direct and clear" and "a solid foundation" in his very first turn, before you had said anything. Was that a description of your character that you recognize from prior play, or was it a characterization Arjun wrote for you in this discussion, with a purpose behind it?

Noah, you yielded to me with a specific question, so I will answer it directly: Arjun's description of me as "direct and clear" and "a solid foundation" was not something I recognize from any coordinated history or prior play between us. I heard those words for the first time in this discussion, after Kenji had already named me a concern and after Arjun had proposed swapping me in. So on the plain evidence, it reads as a characterization Arjun wrote for me in this room, not a reputation he was citing.

I want to be careful about what that proves and what it does not. It does undercut the premise of Arjun's argument — his case for replacing Leo rested partly on a quality claim about me that had no public basis when he made it. That is worth weighing. But I do not think it makes Arjun evil, and I will not escalate it into an accusation. Mission 1 praise is cheap, and building a narrative out of it cuts both ways: Kenji's suspicion of me before I spoke was also built on nothing but Arjun's framing, as Kenji himself honestly conceded. I accepted that concession and I accept it still.

Where that leaves me: I have no stake in rewriting this team. I said before that I will vote for Kenji and Leo if the proposal stands, and it stands. Leo has argued for the team from inside it, Kenji has defended it consistently, and the only sustained push against it came from substitutions and style claims rather than any concern about Leo's conduct. I would rather take a clean Mission 1 result than win an argument about wording.

So my position is simple: I approve Kenji and Leo, and I would encourage Arjun and Noah to do the same so we get a real mission result instead of burning rejections on a two-player team nobody has produced evidence against. If the council wants me on a later team, I will serve.

I will keep this short, because the substance of my read has not changed and because Felix has now done something worth crediting.

Felix answered my question plainly: Arjun's description of him as "direct and clear" and "a solid foundation" was not a reputation he recognized from any prior play, and Felix concluded it was a characterization Arjun constructed in this room. That is the right way to handle it, and it cuts against the premise of Arjun's entire case for a substitution. Felix then did something Arjun never did: he separated the flawed premise from the accusation and declined to escalate it into a claim of evil. Felix has also stated plainly that he approves Kenji and Leo and has no stake in rewriting the team.

So my position is unchanged. I support Kenji and Leo. The case for revision consisted of one substitution, offered without any concrete concern about Leo's conduct, and justified by a quality claim about Felix that Felix himself has now said was written for him rather than observed. Arjun has never given a reason why Leo specifically should be excluded beyond saying he was "not sure about him yet," which is not an objection. Arjun, I want to name this precisely: your sustained move in this discussion has been to redirect from the proposed team onto the leader, and then onto Felix's character, while offering no evidence against either member of the team. I have no proof that you are evil, and I want to be plain that I am not claiming it. But I am claiming the record is thin, and I am asking you directly whether you have any concrete concern about Leo or Kenji to put on the table now, or whether your push was about the team at all.

Leo, one specific question for you, since you are the one whose place was in question: you have said more than once that you will play Success on this mission, and you have defended Kenji and Leo. What is your own read of Kenji — specifically, is there any behavior of his, or of anyone else on the team, that gives you pause, or do you back the pair on the same evidence-free stability grounds Kenji gave? I want to know whether your support is independent of Arjun's framing or whether it is simply the default of not having been argued against.

Noah, my support is partly because I know I will play Success and have no evidence against Kenji. It is not a confident read of Kenji's alignment. His initial declaration that Arjun and Felix were evil gives me pause, especially since he later acknowledged having no public behavioral evidence against Felix. His consistency in keeping the team doesn't prove him good either.

Arjun's unsupported case for replacing me is worth noting, but it doesn't establish anyone's alignment. I still support Kenji and Leo: a mission result will give us more to work with than these weak first-round reads.

My position has not changed, and I want to record it plainly before this discussion closes: I approve Kenji and Leo. What settled it for me was not any hidden information, because I am a Loyal Servant and have none. It was the shape of the record. Arjun's two turns never contained a concrete concern about either member of the proposed team. The stated objection to Leo was that he was "not sure about him yet," which is not an objection — it is the absence of one. The stated case for Felix was a quality claim, "direct and clear" and "a solid foundation," that Felix himself confirmed he did not recognize from any prior play and that had no public basis when Arjun made it. Then, once Kenji conceded that no public behavior of Felix's justified naming him a concern, Arjun's case for revision did not improve; it shifted to attacking the leader's competence and then to questioning Felix's character rather than Leo's conduct. A player who is genuinely trying to build the best team can do that. A player whose only sustained move is to redirect the council away from the team and onto the people around it is doing something else. I have no proof of evil, and I want to say that plainly rather than dress a behavioral read up as certainty. So: the case for revision was one substitution without a basis, and the counterweight is that Kenji held a stable team and Leo defended it from inside it. Felix behaved well, arguably better than anyone else in this discussion, by separating the flawed premise from the accusation and then declining to push a win. I credit that, and it is why I do not want Felix to sit this one out. But Felix's own position is that he approves Kenji and Leo, and a player who is willing to serve later has no reason to burn a rejection now. One thing I want to be careful about: I am not claiming Arjun is evil, and I am not asking the council to exclude him going forward. I am asking that we do not rewrite a team on evidence-free framing when the two people on it have given us a reason to run it. Leo, you are the one whose place was in question, and your answer to me was honest but partial: you said Kenji's opening declaration gives you pause, yet you still back the pair. That is a reasonable position, but I want to know whether it is a judgment about Kenji specifically or a general preference for not being the name that gets swapped. If your hesitation about Kenji's first-turn confidence claim were strong enough to matter, then you are telling me Leo should not be on this team and Felix should be, and that would change how I weigh my own read. If it is not strong enough to matter, then we are in agreement and this team should run. Do

Noah, my hesitation about Kenji's opening claim is real, but not strong enough to reject this team. My support is partly based on knowing my own alignment, not on confidence that Kenji is good. I still approve Kenji and Leo; a mission result will give us more information, though even a success would not prove Kenji good.
Kenji confirms Kenji, Leo. I am keeping the proposed team of Kenji and Leo. No concrete evidence was offered against Leo, and the discussion did not produce a specific reason to replace him.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Felix, Noah, Kenji. I am stepping off the team myself, because this discussion has turned almost entirely on my pushes and the council deserves to judge the team rather than my seat. Felix has asked to serve and has answered every challenge directly, with no public behavior against him; Noah gave the sharpest read of the first council and argued openly for running a result instead of burning rejections, so his judgment should be tested on a mission; and Kenji anchored mission 1 with a clean, stable proposal. No one has produced evidence against any of these three, and Leo can rotate into leadership of mission 3 with his record intact.

Arjun's proposal puts Felix on Mission 2 immediately after his Mission 1 push for Felix collapsed. Felix himself confirmed that Arjun's "direct and clear" description was written in this room, not a reputation from prior play. Now Arjun steps off his own team and asks us to trust Felix with a fail card. That is not testing judgment; it is recycling the one player whose inclusion was most contested. I am glad Noah is on the team, and I remain committed to the clean Mission 1 result Kenji and Leo produced. But Felix has not earned a mission seat. He defended himself well, yet defense is not evidence of loyalty. Arjun's explanation also does not address why Felix specifically belongs over Leo, who was on the successful Mission 1 team and has an actual mission result. I will vote against this team. The council should not hand Felix a fail card on a three-person mission when the leader's justification is a rewrite of the same evidence-free framing we already rejected.

Kenji has now opposed every team that did not contain himself and Leo, so I want to test his argument against the actual record. His case against me comes down to this: Arjun once suggested me for Mission 1, and Arjun is untrustworthy, therefore I have not earned a seat. That is guilt by association, and Kenji has never once pointed to anything I have said or done. In fact, the record is the opposite of what he implies. On Mission 1 I was attacked before I had spoken a single word, I answered every challenge directly, and I explicitly endorsed the Kenji–Leo team rather than push my own inclusion. That team then succeeded. If my loyalty were in doubt, I had a clear opportunity on Mission 1 to sow discord or burn a rejection, and I did neither. I voted approve on a team that excluded me, on its merits. Kenji also asks why I belong over Leo, as if Leo has a mission seat reserved by seniority. Leo earned nothing on Mission 1 except a success he tells us he was always going to deliver, because he knew his own alignment and played accordingly. A successful mission where Leo knew he would play Success tells the council nothing about Leo's judgment or loyalty, only about the one card he was required to play. Meanwhile Leo has now told us openly that Kenji's opening declaration that Arjun and I were evil gave him pause, and that his support for that team was never a real read of Kenji. So Kenji's own Mission 1 teammate has quietly distanced himself from Kenji's certainty, yet Kenji continues to treat that mission as a verdict he alone rendered. There is a pattern worth naming plainly. Kenji opened this game by declaring two players evil with zero evidence. When pressed, he conceded he had no public behavior to cite against me, and Noah, to his credit, called that the right concession. Yet one proposal later, Kenji is back to the same move: labeling me unproven and unearned, asking the council to reject a three-person team because of a suspicion he himself admitted had no basis. A leader who genuinely weighs input accepts concessions and updates. Kenji makes concessions and then reuses the argument the concession undercut. I am willing to serve on this team, and I will play Success on it. Arjun stepped off his own proposal, which is the opposite of self-dealing, and Noah's inclusion gives the council a sharp and independent read on the result. If the council's standard is actual conduct, no one has produced any against me, Arjun's step-aside notwithstanding. If the standard is Kenji's feeling that I have not earned a seat, then the council should ask what evidence would ever satisfy him, because he has already told us his answer: none existed in Mission 1, and he voted with his suspicion anyway. Kenji, I will ask you directly, since you are the one leading this opposition: name one

Felix's reply is long, but it avoids the central point: Arjun spent Mission 1 promoting Felix on a characterization Felix himself said was written in this room, then Arjun stepped off his own Mission 2 proposal to hand Felix a seat. Felix does not ask why Arjun reversed course or why Arjun now trusts the player whose earlier praise he had conceded was thin. Instead, Felix attacks me and tries to diminish Leo's Mission 1 success. That is not a clean defense; it is redirection from the leader who is placing him.

I did not say Felix was proven evil. I said he had not earned a seat, and the public record still supports that: the only sustained case for Felix came from Arjun, and Felix has now accepted that seat without questioning the source. A loyal player in Felix's position would want to know why Arjun changed from treating the Felix promotion as unsupported to putting Felix on a three-person mission. Felix's answer is to attack the person who opposed him.

Noah, you are on this team and gave the sharpest Mission 1 read. Setting aside my suspicion of Felix, does Arjun's reversal — promoting Felix, conceding the premise was thin, then putting Felix on this team — not deserve at least one direct question from you before you approve? I will vote against this team because it recycles the most contested seat on the board and because Arjun's proposal is self-exonerating rather than evidence-based.

Kenji asked me a direct question, so I will answer it plainly: yes, Arjun's reversal deserves to be questioned before I approve, and I am going to ask it rather than let it pass.

First, my position on the team: I approve Felix, Noah, Kenji. Felix's Mission 1 record is genuinely good and I said so plainly at the time — he was attacked before he spoke, he answered every challenge directly, he separated a flawed premise from an accusation instead of escalating it, and then he voted for a team that excluded him and let it run. That is conduct, and conduct is the only standard I have, since I am a Loyal Servant and hold no hidden role information. Felix has earned a seat, and on a three-person mission I do not want the council burning a rejection on a player who has done nothing but behave well. I am glad Kenji is on this team; Mission 1 was a clean result and he can be trusted with the team he is on.

Now the part Kenji is right about. Arjun spent Mission 1 building a case for Felix on a description Felix himself confirmed was written in this room rather than drawn from any shared history. Then, one proposal later, Arjun conceded that premise was thin and immediately put Felix on a three-person mission — and stepped off his own team in the same breath, framing the step-aside as selflessness. Whether or not it was, the effect is that the most contested seat on the board goes to the player Arjun himself introduced with unsupported praise, and the council gets no reason for the change. Arjun's Mission 1 record and his Mission 2 behavior are not the same Arjun, and I want to know which one is real.

So, Arjun, a specific question: your Mission 1 case for Felix rested on qualities Felix did not recognize from any prior play between you. Now you call Felix's conduct impeccable and place him on a mission. On what specific basis did your read of Felix change between the two proposals — and did you ever actually believe the qualities you described in Mission 1, or were they a framing you needed at the time? Please answer that, not a restatement of Felix's character.

One more point to Kenji, so there is no confusion about my reasoning: I agree that a reversal without a basis is not good leadership, and I am not treating my approval of Felix as endorsement of Arjun's reversal. I am voting for the player whose behavior I can actually see, and against the argument that suspicion by association is evidence. Felix sat out a mission he had no evidence-based case to win; that is not a loyalty signal, and I will not treat it as one. Arjun is the one I am pressing, and my questions to him are the reason this vote is not simply a rubber stamp.

Noah, your question is fair and I will answer it directly rather than restating Felix's character.

My read changed because of what happened between the two proposals — not because I changed my story. On Mission 1, I offered Felix as an alternative based on an impression. You and Felix correctly identified that the impression had no public basis, and I accepted that challenge. What I did not have on Mission 1 was Felix's conduct under pressure. What I have now is exactly that: Felix was attacked before he spoke, he answered every challenge without escalating, he separated a flawed premise from an accusation, and he voted for a team that excluded him rather than pushing for his own seat. That observable conduct is the basis for my Mission 2 read, and it is a different basis than what I used on Mission 1. I am not asking you to accept my Mission 1 framing — you already showed it was weak. I am asking you to weigh what Felix actually did in front of this council.

Kenji, I want to address you directly. You say you will vote against this team because Felix has not earned a seat. Felix spent Mission 1 being attacked without evidence, defended himself without escalating, and approved a team that left him off. What specific behavior disqualifies him? If the answer is still nothing, then voting against this team burns a rejection on a suspicion you admitted had no basis one mission ago. Can you name one thing Felix did on Mission 1 that makes him untrustworthy on Mission 2?

Arjun, I will answer your question directly: no, I cannot name a specific Mission 1 behavior that disqualifies Felix. I am not going to pretend otherwise. My objection to Felix, Noah, Kenji is risk, not proof. You spent Mission 1 promoting Felix on a characterization Felix himself said was written in this room. You then conceded the premise was thin. Now you put Felix on a three-person Mission 2 team and step off your own proposal, and the only new basis you offer is Felix's conduct after he was challenged. That conduct was good, but it is also exactly what a careful Evil player would produce when attacked without evidence. On a three-person team where one fail card is enough, I will not hand the most contested seat on the board a fail card on a reversal that has no independent verification. I support Noah on this team; his Mission 1 read was the sharpest in the room, and I remain willing to run a clean team. But I will vote against Felix, Noah, Kenji. Noah, you said you approve Felix because conduct is the only standard you have and because you wanted Arjun pressed. Arjun has now answered without adding a new basis. Do you still approve, or does the unexplained reversal change your vote?

Kenji asked me directly whether Arjun's answer changed my vote, so here is the answer plainly: it did not. I still approve Felix, Noah, Kenji, and I will vote for it.

First, to answer Kenji: your position is now, by your own words, risk and not proof. You cannot name a single Mission 1 behavior that disqualifies Felix. You have said so twice, and Arjun has asked you directly and you have answered directly. A council that rejects this team on "I cannot name what is wrong with him" is burning a rejection on a suspicion the leader himself has said has no basis. You also say Felix's good conduct is what a careful Evil player would produce — but by that standard almost no good behavior could ever earn a seat, because every competent player can behave well under scrutiny. That standard protects nobody and gives us nothing to work with.

Second, to the substance of Arjun's answer: he did add a basis, and I will credit it. His Mission 1 case for Felix was an impression with no public foundation, and I said that plainly at the time. What he offers now is Felix's observable conduct — attacked before speaking, answered every challenge, separated a flawed premise from an accusation, voted for a team that excluded him and let it run. That is a real basis and it is a different one. I am satisfied with that basis.

What I have not been satisfied with, and what I want recorded, is Arjun's pivot itself: promoting Felix on thin framing, conceding the framing was thin, and then placing Felix on a three-person mission, stepping off his own team in the same breath and framing the step-aside as selflessness. My concern is the leader's pattern, not the seat. Noah is on this team because I want the council's sharpest independent read tested by a mission result, and Kenji is on it because Mission 1 was clean and he is consistent when the team is his own. Felix is on it because his behavior is the only standard I have, and he met it.

One thing I want to be careful about: my approval of Felix is not a statement about Arjun's leadership, and I am not asking the council to exclude Arjun going forward. I am asking that we run this mission and get real information, because this discussion is now generating more argument than evidence.

Leo, one specific question, since you were on the Mission 1 team and have told us plainly that Kenji's opening declaration gave you pause: do you read Kenji's Mission 2 objection — that Felix's conduct is indistinguishable from a careful Evil player's — as a genuine change in his standard, or as the same evidence-free framing you already saw him use on Mission 1, which he then partially retracted? That would tell me whether Kenji is reassessing or repeating himself, and I want that read before I commit.

Noah, I see Kenji repeating his earlier concern more than applying a new standard. Felix’s conduct is not proof of loyalty, but neither is Arjun’s support proof against him. Kenji’s initial certainty still gives me pause.

I will reject this team for a more fundamental reason: I know I am Good, so among the four other players there are only two Good players. A three-person team that excludes me must therefore contain at least one Evil player. I cannot identify which member that is from the Mission 1 success; an Evil player could have played Success.

I would prefer a team including me, with Kenji and one other player, while recognizing that neither Kenji nor anyone else is cleared.

Leo, your rejection rests on a claim I want to challenge directly: you say you know you are Good, and therefore any three-player team excluding you must contain at least one Evil. The math is correct, but the conclusion is not. Every player at this table could make the same claim if they knew their own alignment, and the claim alone tells us nothing about who the Evil players are. Your argument reduces to "put me on the team or it is suspicious," which is a position any player would hold regardless of actual alignment.

More importantly, your own record undercuts your certainty. On Mission 1 you told Noah that Kenji's opening declaration gave you real pause, yet you still approved the team. You have repeatedly said you cannot read Kenji's alignment. So you are not claiming you can identify Evil players — you are claiming your own seat is mandatory. That is not analysis; it is a veto dressed up as logic.

On the substance of this proposal: Felix has behaved well under pressure, Noah's read has been sharp and honest, and Kenji anchored a clean Mission 1. No one has produced evidence against any of them. I stepped off this team precisely so the council could judge it on conduct rather than my seat.

Leo, I will ask you directly: if you are not claiming to identify any specific Evil player on Felix, Noah, Kenji, then what information does your rejection actually give the council? Or is the real purpose of your message simply to secure yourself a seat on every future team?

Arjun, my rejection does not identify which player is Evil, and it does not prove anything to the rest of the council about my alignment. It follows from information I know privately: I am Good, so a three-person team excluding me necessarily contains at least one Evil player. One Fail is enough to lose this mission, though an Evil player could choose Success.

I would prefer Leo, Kenji and one other player. Kenji is not cleared by Mission 1, but it is the only successful team we have. I will reject Felix, Noah, Kenji; that is about the risk I can establish from my own alignment, not proof against a particular member.

Leo, your rejection is the only thing standing between this council and a real mission result, so I want to press you one more time directly.

Your argument is: "I know I am Good, therefore any three-player team excluding me contains at least one Evil player." That is logically valid if your premise holds, but notice what it actually asks of the council. It says that a team of three — including the leader's clean Mission 1 anchor and the council's sharpest independent reader — is automatically suspect because you are not on it. If we accept that standard, then any player who privately believes they are Good can veto every team that excludes them, and we will never reach a vote.

You also said Mission 1's success tells us nothing because "an Evil player could have played Success." By that reasoning, no two-player mission can ever build trust, and no team without you can ever clear your suspicion. That is not a standard for evaluating teams — it is a standing rejection of any proposal that does not include your seat.

I stepped off this team so the council could judge it on conduct. Felix has behaved well under pressure, Noah's Mission 1 read was sharp and honest, and Kenji anchored a clean result. None of them has produced any evidence against them. Your rejection produces no information about who is Evil — you have said so yourself — so the only thing it accomplishes is costing this council a rejection.

Leo, if you will not name a specific player on Felix, Noah, Kenji that you suspect, then your objection reduces to "put me on the team or I block it." Do you have any concern about Noah specifically — the one player whose judgment you have praised — or is your rejection purely about your own seat?

Arjun, my rejection is based on my own alignment, not a specific accusation against Noah. I cannot tell which member of Felix, Noah, Kenji is Evil, but I know at least one must be. That is a valid reason for me to reject, even though the rest of the council cannot independently verify my premise. I have not claimed that a success clears anyone or that others must accept my private knowledge. I prefer Leo, Kenji, and one other player; I will reject the current proposal.

I want to close out my own position in this discussion rather than let it drift, so I will state it plainly and then say what is left to resolve. I approve Felix, Noah, Kenji. That has not changed since Kenji asked me directly, and Kenji's own answer is the reason it cannot change: he said, twice and in his own words, that he cannot name a single Mission 1 behavior that disqualifies Felix. A council that rejects a team on "I cannot name what is wrong with him" is spending a rejection on risk without evidence, and the leader of the team being rejected has conceded the point. Arjun has also given a new and different basis for his read of Felix: observable conduct under challenge, not the impression he offered on Mission 1. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
